title: Decide who will run the service after delivery
focus: The useful difference is operational responsibility. With drop-off, someone at your office needs to receive the food, set it out, replenish the table and clear the space. A staffed booking can assign those responsibilities to an agreed team. Compare the formats against the length of your event and the facilities available, not just the price per person. A short team lunch may need little support, while a client reception benefits from coordinated service throughout the event.

sections.title: Make the delivery handover clear
paragraphs: For food-only delivery, nominate someone who will receive the order and confirm the handover details. Share the exact address, access instructions and requested delivery window. If the location is inside a larger building, include the floor, reception process and any restrictions on deliveries.

Know what happens next. Your team may need to arrange the food, provide serving items, replenish the table and handle clear-down. Ask which packaging, labels and serving guidance are included, and check whether any equipment is supplied or needs to be arranged separately.

The menu should suit the interval between delivery and eating. Tell the team if food will be served later or in several stages so the request can be assessed appropriately. Follow the dish-specific instructions provided at handover and ask for clarification where needed. A clear delivery arrangement gives you convenience without leaving important responsibilities undefined.

sections.title: Choose the support that makes hosting easier
paragraphs: Decide who will do the work after the food arrives. If your own team will lay out platters, replenish drinks and clear the space, a delivery arrangement may be suitable. If you want to stay with your guests, discuss setup, service staff, equipment and clear-down as part of the proposal.

Different formats create different demands. A buffet needs attention to presentation and replenishment; a plated meal requires coordination between the kitchen and table; passed food needs staff who can circulate comfortably through the room. The number of guests matters, but so do the layout and pace of service.

Ask for included roles and hours to be clearly identified. Additional items such as table linen, crockery, glassware, bar support or styling should be confirmed explicitly. A well-defined scope lets you understand the service you are buying and helps the team prepare for the work you expect.

sections.title: Keep catering aligned with the business agenda
paragraphs: Share the event programme with the catering brief. Registration, meeting sessions, networking and presentations create different service opportunities. Food should support those moments: easy-to-eat options for a working break, a more relaxed selection for networking or a seated meal when guests have time to enjoy it.

Confirm who will approve the menu and who will coordinate access on the day. The billing contact may be different from the person at the venue, so include both roles where relevant. If your organisation needs particular supplier documents, purchase-order references or invoice details, raise them before the booking is finalised.

A practical service plan also considers the return to work. Collection, waste handling and clear-down should fit the venue's schedule. When the catering is connected to the agenda and responsibilities are clear, the team can deliver a professional experience without drawing attention away from the purpose of the event.
